title: # Leadership, Halakha and Social Reform: The Work and Torah Teachings of Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache (HaḤaBYaF)
source_file: מנהיגות, הלכה ותיקון חברתי_ פועלו ומשנתו התורנית של רבי חיים פלאג_י (החבי_ף).docx
content:
Leadership, Halakhah, and Social Reform: The Work and Halakhic Scholarship of Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache (HaḤaBYP)

This survey traces the life and halakhic scholarship of Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache (HaḤaBYP), one of the greatest halakhic decisors and leaders of Sephardic Jewry in nineteenth-century Izmir. The text emphasizes how, alongside phenomenal literary productivity encompassing dozens of works integrating halakhah and Kabbalah, HaḤaBYP functioned as a radical social leader who struggled for social justice through reforms in communal taxation and compulsory education ordinances for children. Beyond his religious standing as "Ḥakham Bashi," the source describes the extraordinary official recognition he received from the Ottoman government, illustrating his decisive influence in shaping the modern character of the Jewish community. The article summarizes his legacy as a rare combination of conservative halakhic authority and deep humane sensitivity, which transformed Torah into an instrument for social repair and public health.

Leadership, Halakhah, and Social Reform: The Work and Halakhic Scholarship of Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache (HaḤaBYP)

Biographical Introduction and Family Background in Izmir

Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache, known in halakhic and historical literature as HaḤaBYP or MoHaRḤP, is considered one of the greatest halakhic decisors and leaders of Sephardic Jewry in the nineteenth century.[1, 2, 3] He was active in the city of Izmir in the Ottoman Empire, which at that time was a vibrant spiritual and cultural center.[2, 4] HaḤaBYP was born into a distinguished and influential family; his father, Rabbi Ya'akov Palache, was a renowned rabbi and kabbalist, and his mother, Qali Qadin, was the daughter of the generational leader Rabbi Yosef Refa'el ben Ḥayyim Ḥazan.[4, 5] The grandfather, author of the monumental responsa work Ḥiqrei Lev (Inquiries of the Heart), served at the end of his life as Rishon le-Tsiyon in Jerusalem and was the central figure who shaped his grandson's education, public standing, and halakhic approach.[4, 5]

Rabbi Ḥayyim's diligence in childhood and youth became legendary in his life story. Various biographical testimonies note that from early youth until reaching age twenty he never ceased studying day and night, while avoiding all interruption from Torah study.[4, 6] He acquired his fundamental learning at Yeshivat Beit Ya'akov Rabbi in Izmir, where he studied under the guidance of the generation's leading scholars, including Rabbi Yitsḥaq Mayo, Rabbi Yitsḥaq Gattegno, and Rabbi Pinḥas Refa'el Yehoshu'a di Segura.[4, 6, 7] At age nineteen he married Esterola, daughter of the notable Rabbi Yitsḥaq Rabbi, one of the yeshivah's principal financial supporters.[4, 6] This marriage into a household of Torah and prominence enabled him to continue devoting himself to study without the burden of earning a living.[6]

Historical research points to several chronological discrepancies in various sources concerning the dates of HaḤaBYP's birth and death, as well as regarding the precise age at which he was appointed to his various positions. This lack of clarity typically stems from the complex transition between the different calendars (Hebrew, Julian, and Gregorian) that were current in the Ottoman Empire and Europe during that period.

Family Dynasty and Imperial Status in the Tanzimat Era

Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache's period of leadership largely coincided with the "Tanzimat era" in the Ottoman Empire, a period characterized by modern reforms, increased governmental centralization, and reorganization of the status of religious minorities.[4, 5] Against this background, HaḤaBYP's official appointment as Ḥakham Bashi in the year 5616 (1855) was not merely an internal religious event, but received formal imperial endorsement through a royal decree (nişan) granted to him by Sultan Abdülmecid I.[4, 9] This decree conferred upon him extensive de facto judicial and enforcement powers, including supervision of tax collection and administration of public order with the assistance of Ottoman security forces.[4, 9]

From a familial perspective, HaḤaBYP headed an illustrious rabbinic dynasty that continued to lead the community with distinction.[5] He raised three sons who were all prominent Torah scholars: Rabbi Avraham, Rabbi Yitsḥaq (Raḥamim Nissim), and Rabbi Yosef.[4, 5] The sons held conservative worldviews similar to their father's and steadfastly opposed the penetration of modern Western influences, such as adoption of European dress style among community members.[5] The two elder sons subsequently inherited his position in the city's leadership.[5] Additionally, his grandson (son of Rabbi Ya'akov), named after him Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache II, continued the dynasty of instruction and served as rosh yeshivah at the central yeshivot Beit Hillel and Beit Ya'akov Rabbi.[3] HaḤaBYP's exalted public standing was also expressed in the conferral of the prestigious imperial honor "Order of the Mecidiye Third Class" by the Ottoman authorities, an unprecedented recognition for a Jewish leader at that time.[5]

HaḤaBYP's Literary Empire and Halakhic Scholarship

Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache is considered among the most prolific authors in the history of halakhic and Jewish intellectual literature in the Aḥaronim period.[2, 4] His literary arsenal includes between 70 and 80 books encompassing all branches of halakhic creativity: Bible, Talmud, midrash, halakhah, Kabbalah, and ethics.[1, 4, 5, 8] HaḤaBYP was accustomed to writing his books while studying at Yeshivat Beit Hillel, where he composed most of his works.[4, 5, 8]

Under his authorship, responsa literature (she'elot u-teshuvot) acquired an international dimension; halakhic inquiries were addressed to him from distant communities in Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East.[4, 5, 8] A striking example of the bibliographic complexity of his books is the monumental responsa work Lev Ḥayyim (Heart of Life).[5, 10] The book, whose first volume was printed when he was thirty-two years old, suffered in its original form from severe printing problems—broken and worn letters that made study extremely difficult.[2, 10] Moreover, the book's sections were not originally arranged according to the customary order of the four parts of the Shulḥan 'Arukh, which created significant difficulty in locating material for judges and decisors.[10] Only in later generations, within the framework of publishers' initiatives such as Ahavat Shalom, was the book reprinted in handsome editions that corrected these deficiencies and added detailed indices.[10]

HaḤaBYP's adjudicatory methodology combined the formal world of halakhah with the world of the concealed and Kabbalah.[2] He relied on the hierarchical rules of halakhic decision-making that had crystallized among the Sephardic sages, particularly those formulated in the Kenesset ha-Gedolah (The Great Assembly) by Rabbi Ḥayyim Benveniste.[11] These rules instruct that when the Zohar and the kabbalists disagree with the Talmud and the halakhic decisors—one should rule according to the Gemara.[11, 12] Nevertheless, in cases where there is no explicit ruling in the Talmud, or when controversy exists among the decisors, the words of Kabbalah and the Zohar serve as the deciding factor.[11, 12] From this methodology emerged his books of religious conduct, such as Kaf ha-Ḥayyim (Palm of Life) and Mo'ed le-Khol Ḥai (Festival for All the Living), which integrate pure halakhah with kabbalistic intentions in performing commandments and ethical conduct.[2, 4, 5, 13]

Social Reforms, Public Health, and Practical Leadership

HaḤaBYP's persona was etched in public memory not only as a detached halakhic genius, but as a courageous and radical social leader who fought fiercely for the weaker classes.[4, 8] His leadership placed social justice, children's education, and public health at the center, while using his Torah authority to impose structural changes in the community.

Tax Battles and the Gabela Polemic

One of the most important reforms that Rabbi Ḥayyim led was the polemic over the meat tax (the gabela).[4] The custom of communities at that time was to impose a heavy indirect tax on kosher slaughter to finance communal institutions, a tax that weighed especially on the poor while the wealthy avoided paying progressive direct taxes.[4] Rabbi Ḥayyim went forth in battle against the wealthy, accusing them of placing the community's burden on the shoulders of the poor.[4]

He established an unequivocal halakhic ruling that part of the gabela revenues must be allocated directly to financing the education of poor children and supporting Torah scholars.[4] He clarified that collecting tax from meat without such allocation
and was considered "robbery and violence."[4] This audacious ruling triggered severe political and economic confrontations with the leadership of the wealthy notables in the city, but the Ḥabi"f stood resolutely by his position.[4]

Ordinance of Compulsory Education and Child Protection

Rabbi Ḥayyim was ahead of his time in creating a social-educational safety net for children.[4] He enacted a communal ordinance constituting a type of "compulsory education" law, according to which fathers were forbidden to withdraw their sons from educational institutions and send them to work as apprentices with artisans at a young age.[4]

Rabbi Ḥayyim determined that a youth was not permitted to begin working unless he had completed his basic studies in the Talmud Torah and knew how to read and master the order of prayer completely.[4] For this purpose, special supervisory committees were established that examined the youths and authorized their entry into the labor market only after they met the requirements.[4] In order to enable poor families to comply with this ordinance, the Ḥabi"f ensured the establishment of support funds and special yeshivot in which students received respectable subsistence stipends for the maintenance of their households.[4]

Public Health Ordinances and Practical Halakhic Leadership

Another domain in which his innovative rulings were prominent was public health.[4, 8] The Ḥabi"f was among the first posekim to warn against the harms of smoking and addiction to tobacco and strong drink.[9] He enacted a public ordinance calling for abstention from smoking cigarettes not only on the Sabbath but even on weekdays due to the health hazard involved.[4, 8]

In his book Kaf ha-Ḥayyim ("Palm of Life," siman 11, halakhah 19), the Ḥabi"f addressed a practical issue combining health, religious quorum, and human relations: the custom of inhaling tobacco snuff in the synagogue.[15] The Ḥabi"f ruled that it is forbidden to inhale tobacco in the synagogue during prayer and the ḥazzan's repetition in order to preserve the sanctity of prayer and cleanliness, and if a person gives tobacco to his fellow, he must do so in a backhanded manner to prevent frivolity.[15] Nevertheless, he qualified and permitted the distribution of tobacco at times that are not designated prayer times (such as during the auction of miṣvot), out of a profound sociological understanding that this custom "increases peace" and brings together the hearts of the worshippers.[15]

The Final Days and Passing of the Ḥabi"f

Toward the end of his days, upon reaching the age of seventy (in the year 5617 [1857]), the Ḥabi"f resolved in his heart to leave Izmir and ascend to the Holy Land, an aspiration that had accompanied him all his life.[4] However, word of his intention to leave stirred turmoil among the members of the community; the notables of the city and its sages implored him not to abandon them at this time, and he yielded to their entreaties and remained on the rabbinical seat in Izmir.[4]

On Simḥat Torah of the year 5628 (1867), when he ascended to the Torah and read the verse "And Moses died there" with heartrending weeping, the members of the community sensed that their leader was taking leave of them and that his end was near.[4] In the month of Shevat of that year, the Ḥabi"f completed the writing of his final book Birkat Mo'adekha le-Ḥayyim ("May Your Appointed Times Be Blessed for Life"), as he signed the writing of the introduction only one day before his passing.[2, 4] On the final night of his life he performed tikkun ḥaṣot with weeping and anguish over the exile of the Shekhinah, and on the 17th of Shevat 5628 (February 10, 1868) he returned his soul to his Creator at a ripe old age.[2, 4, 9]

The funeral procession of Rabbi Ḥayyim Palaggi is considered one of the impressive historical events in the annals of Turkish Jewry. Extraordinary state honors were accorded him by the Ottoman government; an armed battalion of Turkish army soldiers accompanied his coffin, an honor granted to only two or three chief rabbis throughout the history of the empire.[4, 5, 9] His funeral was attended by throngs of worshippers, the rabbis of the city, and diplomatic representatives of foreign countries, with the crowd marching with lit candles and carrying dozens of his books.[4, 5, 8]

He was buried in the ancient Jewish cemetery in Izmir.[4, 5, 8] His gravestone is the only one in the entire cemetery facing eastward (while the other gravestones face south), a biographical-archaeological singularity whose halakhic or kabbalistic reason remains a mystery to this day.[4]

Summary

The activity and teaching of Rabbi Ḥayyim Palaggi reflect a combination of conservative and uncompromising halakhic authority on the one hand, and profound social sensitivity and reformist spirit on the other hand. In an era of acute political and cultural transformations, the Ḥabi"f did not retreat into the four cubits of halakhah, but rather transformed Jewish law into a ministerial instrument for the accomplishment of social justice, protection of children, struggle against economic tyranny, and preservation of public health. The written legacy he left behind—dozens of books that serve to this day as foundational works in pesikah and thought—alongside the dynasty of leadership he established, confirm his status as one of the most influential leaders in shaping the face of Sephardic and Oriental Jewry in the modern era.

content:
The Work, Leadership, and Halakhic Teachings of Ha-Ḥaviv"f (Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache)

This text surveys the life history and monumental contribution of Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache (Ha-Ḥaviv"f), who was among the most prominent spiritual and communal leaders in Sephardic Jewry in the nineteenth century. The article sketches his profile as a multifaceted personality who combined profound halakhic erudition, expertise in esoteric Torah, and extensive political activity vis-à-vis the Ottoman government on behalf of the community in Smyrna. Among the central topics in the text, his enormous literary enterprise stands out, encompassing more than seventy compositions, as well as his distinctive method of halakhic decision-making that prefers the principle of "halakhah aḥaronah" and integrates the revealed realm with Kabbalah. In addition, the source emphasizes his modern social leadership, which found expression in the establishment of charitable and medical institutions and in public ordinances to improve the health and welfare of the poor.

The Work, Leadership, and Halakhic Teachings of Ha-Ḥaviv"f (Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache)

Genealogical Lineage, Family Background, and Stages of His Torah Development

Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache the Second, known in the Torah world by the acronym Ha-Ḥaviv"f (Ha-Gaon Rabbi Ḥayyim ben Ya'akov Palache), stands as one of the greatest and most prolific decisors, kabbalists, and halakhic leaders of Sephardic Jewry in the era of the Aḥaronim.[1, 2, 3] His work, which spanned most of the nineteenth century in the city of Smyrna in the Ottoman Empire, was characterized by a rare fusion of profound Talmudic erudition, extensive kabbalistic expertise, and active communal leadership in an era of transformations and modernization.[1, 2]

Ha-Ḥaviv"f was born in Smyrna on 17 Tevet 5548 (28 January 1788) to an illustrious family of sages, and was named after his grandfather, Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache the First, who was the father of Rabbi Ya'akov.[1, 2, 3] His father, Rabbi Ya'akov Palache, was a renowned kabbalist and among the sages of the yeshiva "Beit Ya'akov Bi Rav."[2, 3] His mother, Kali Kadin (or Kali Kadin Ḥazan), was the daughter of one of the greatest halakhic decisors of his generation—Rabbi Rafa'el Yosef Ḥazan, author of the book Ḥikrei Lev (Ha-Ḥak"l), who served as rabbi of Smyrna and later immigrated to the Land of Israel and served as Rishon le-Tsiyon.[1, 2, 3]

In his childhood and youth he distinguished himself by exceptional diligence; he testified about himself that from age twenty he did not cease from his study day and night without any suspension of Torah study whatsoever.[1] He studied under the tutelage of his grandfather, the Ḥikrei Lev, and of renowned Smyrna sages such as Rabbi Yitsḥak ben Elyakim Gattegno and Rabbi Pinḥas Di Sigura.[1, 2, 3] In the year 5567 (1807), at age nineteen, he married Esther, daughter of Yitsḥak Rabi.[1, 2, 3] After the death of Esther in the year 5594 (1834), Ha-Ḥaviv"f married a second time in the year 5601 (1841) to Vida Neḥama.[3]

In the year 5573 (1813), when he was twenty-five years old, he was ordained by his grandfather with the exalted title "Ha-Ḥakham ha-Shalem" and was invested with the traditional scholars' robe.[1, 3] With the death of his father in the year 5588 (1828), he began to serve officially as a judge and as head of the yeshiva "Beit Ya'akov Rabi," and also taught at the yeshiva "Ets ha-Ḥayyim" where his grandfather had taught.[1, 3] Most of his Torah compositions he wrote at the yeshiva "Beit Hillel" in the city.[1, 3] In the year 5597 (1837) he was appointed as head of the great rabbinical court in Smyrna, and in the year 5615 (1855) he reached the peak of his communal influence with his appointment to the office of "Ha-Ḥakham Bashi" (Chief Rabbi) of Smyrna.[1, 2, 3]

His three sons were also distinguished Torah scholars and prominent leaders who continued the dynasty of leadership and Torah creativity in Smyrna and beyond: Rabbi Avraham Palache (author of Va-Yikra Avraham), Rabbi Raḥamim Nissim Yitsḥak Palache (author of Yafeh la-Lev), and Rabbi Yosef Palache (author of Yosef et Eḥav).[2, 3, 4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Communal and Political Leadership in the Era of Transformations

The leadership of Rabbi Ḥayyim Palache occurred against the background of the "Tanzimat" period—an era of liberal and legal reforms in the Ottoman Empire.[2] Ha-Ḥaviv"f succeeded in exploiting his official status and his diplomatic connections with the central government to fortify the status of the Jewish community, to protect its poor, and to reshape anew the public life patterns in Smyrna.[1, 3]

In the year 5615 (1855) Ha-Ḥaviv"f was appointed to the office of "Chief Communal Rabbi" and "Ha-Ḥakham Bashi" of Smyrna.[1, 3] A year thereafter, in the year 5616, he received official appointment from the Ottoman Sultan Abdülmecid I, which granted him extensive civil and religious authorities for managing the community with a firm hand.[1, 3] These authorities were expanded even further with the accession of the next Sultan.[3] As recognition for his communal and political work, the Ottoman government bestowed upon him the official honor decoration "of the Order of the Mecidiye" third class (Mecidiye Order Third Class).[2]

Under the leadership of Ha-Ḥaviv"f, the community was required to confront difficult internal and external challenges. In the second half of the nineteenth century, relations between the Jewish community and the Greek population in Smyrna progressively worsened, and during the years 1864–1901, six severe incidents of anti-Jewish blood libels occurred in the city.[4] Ha-Ḥaviv"f was required to implement assertive and close policy vis-à-vis the Ottoman authorities in order to ensure the protection of the community against pogroms.[3, 4]

Even earlier, during the severe blood libels in Damascus and Rhodes in the year 5600 (1840), Ha-Ḥaviv"f activated his diplomatic connections and persuaded Sir Moses Montefiore to act for the cancellation of the decrees.[3] Following this joint activity, deep relations of friendship were woven between the two, and Montefiore donated generously to the charitable institutions of Ha-Ḥaviv"f in Smyrna.[3] In his honor and in honor of his wife Judith, Ha-Ḥaviv"f composed the book Derakhav le-Moshe (or Derakhav le-Ḥayyim le-Moshe Tehillah), in which he described the Damascus affair and the work of the activists to rescue the community.[3, 5] Likewise, he composed in the Ladino language (Spanish) the pamphlet Matsa Ḥayyim in honor of the Queen of England, Victoria, as a token of appreciation for her active political involvement in protecting the Jews, while comparing her to Bithiah daughter of Pharaoh who saved Moses from the river.[3, 5] The political intercession of Ha-Ḥaviv"f on behalf of the community nearly cost him his life, when in one incident one of the king's ministers struck him severely.[3]

In the internal communal arena, Ha-Ḥaviv"f worked tirelessly to establish unity in the ranks and on behalf of the poor.[1] He established many welfare institutions for the poor of his city and called for vigilance in honoring them.[1] With the assistance of Moses Montefiore and Baron Benjamin Rothschild, Ha-Ḥaviv"f established a modern Jewish hospital in Smyrna that was intended to provide advanced medical services to the entire public.[1, 3, 6] Likewise, he established a kollel for excellent scholars so that they could devote their time to Torah with economic prosperity and without the burden of livelihood concerns, and even served as arbitrator and sole judge for settling disputes, quarrels, and marital peace problems in the community.[3, 6]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Social and Health Ordinances

The leadership conception of Ha-Ḥaviv"f was not limited to the religious-cultic sphere, but encompassed everyday aspects of bodily and mental health. He became famous for his precedent-setting ordinances against snuffing tobacco, drinking hard liquor, and smoking cigarettes, out of deep awareness of the harms of addiction and the damage to body and soul.[3, 6]

His distinctive ordinance forbidding smoking on Shabbat rested on an original halakhic-psychological argument: Ha-Ḥaviv"f explained that the addicted smoker experiences suffering, distress, and deep mental anguish on Shabbat because of his forced abstention from smoking, and thereby he desecrates and forfeits the commandment of "oneg Shabbat."[3] For this reason, he called to refrain from smoking and snuffing tobacco entirely on Shabbat, and even instructed the public to reduce or abstain from smoking on weekdays for health reasons and prevention of addiction harmful to the body.[1, 6]

In his book Masa Ḥayyim, dealing with laws of statecraft, communal agreements, ordinances, and taxes, Ha-Ḥaviv"f anchored the authority of the rabbinic leadership to enact binding civil and health ordinances, from
and a holistic perspective that connects observance of the commandments with protection of public health and the physical welfare of community members.[5, 7]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

His Halakhic Doctrine: "Halakha Aḥarona" and the Relationship Between Nigleh and Nistar

The halakhic doctrine of Rabbi Ḥayyim Palachi is characterized by exceptional breadth and a consolidated methodology. He responded to hundreds of questions addressed to him from all corners of the world—from Egypt, Libya, and Morocco, through Jerusalem, Tunisia, and Syria, to Ashkenazic communities in Germany, Holland, France, Russia, Poland, and Switzerland.[3, 8] This fact testifies to the global recognition he received as a supreme halakhic authority bridging ritual and cultural gaps between East and West.[3]

The Principle of "Halakha Aḥarona"

In his methodology of halakhic decision-making, the Ḥayyim Palachi distinctly represents the approach favoring the principle of "halakha aḥarona" (the law follows later authorities) over "halakha rishona."[9] He accorded decisive weight to later codification, primarily the Shulḥan Arukh and its commentators, based on a conception that later decisors weigh all the opinions of the Rishonim and produce consolidated rulings adapted to contemporary reality.[9] The Ḥayyim Palachi absolutely preferred the rulings appearing in the Beit Yosef and the Shulḥan Arukh, while rejecting the approach that attempts to bypass the Shulḥan Arukh through direct recourse to the Rishonim who preceded it.[9]

Integration of Halakha and Qabbalah

A central issue in the Ḥayyim Palachi's doctrine is the integration of esoteric teachings and the Zohar within the fabric of practical halakhic adjudication.[1, 10] As a distinguished Qabbalist, the Ḥayyim Palachi accorded immense importance to the Sefer ha-Zohar and the writings of the Ari, but operated under a rigid and sophisticated system of rules for resolving instances of conflict between nigleh and nistar [1, 10]:

Direct dispute between Qabbalah and Talmud/decisors: Where the Zohar or Qabbalistic authorities directly contradict the Babylonian Talmud and the major decisors, it is determined that one must follow the Talmud and the decisors.[10] However, if the Qabbalistic teachings prescribe stricter conduct, it is proper and fitting to be stringent according to Qabbalah.[10]

Silence of the Talmud and decisors: In cases where a particular law is not mentioned at all in the Gemara and decisorial literature but is mentioned in Qabbalistic writings and the Zohar, one should conduct oneself according to the Qabbalistic teachings (though the public is not compelled to do so if it does not wish to).[10]

Resolving disputes among decisors: Where decisors disagreed in their opinions and reached no resolution, the weight of Qabbalistic teachings and the Zohar comes to the fore, and they serve as a deciding factor tilting toward one side of the halakhic equation.[10]

Doubtful blessings and Qabbalah: The broad halakhic principle of "safek berakhot le-hakel" is sometimes applied even against rulings of the Shulḥan Arukh or the teachings of the Ari, while examining the complex relationship between the Ari's instructions and the rules of halakhic doubt.[10]

The Ḥayyim Palachi viewed Torah writing as a holy act with metaphysical dimensions. He customarily recited a special prayer of "le-shem yiḥud" before writing any halakhic responsum, legal ruling, or halakhic clarification, in order to purify his thought from any personal bias or error.[3] Likewise, out of sacred dread and concern for public welfare, he customarily prayed every Sabbath eve that no mishap occur through him and that they not need to violate the Sabbath in Izmir due to life-threatening illness.[3]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Monumental Literary Enterprise and the Catastrophe of the Fire

Rabbi Ḥayyim Palachi was among the most prolific writers in the history of rabbinic literature. He began composing books already at age seventeen (when he wrote his work Pe'ulat Ṣaddiq le-Ḥayyim on Tractate Avot) and continued writing continuously until his final day.[1, 3, 5]

However, his literary enterprise suffered a devastating blow in the year 5601 (1841/1840), when a massive fire raged through Izmir and consumed extensive portions of the Jewish residential quarter.[3] In this disaster, approximately fifty-four volumes of manuscripts ready for press that the Ḥayyim Palachi had written were burned.[3] The traumatic event brought the rabbi to illness from excessive grief, but an exceptional demonstration of spiritual resilience and assistance from his eldest son, Rabbi Avraham, enabled him to reconstruct from memory and from partial notes a substantial portion of the lost writings.[3]

In total, more than seventy books were printed during his lifetime and posthumously, encompassing all parts of the Torah: Bible, Mishnah, Babylonian and Palestinian Talmud, halakha, responsa, Qabbalah, Midrash, ethics, and prayers.[1, 5] Nearly all his books bear in their titles the word "Ḥayyim," as an allusion to his given name and as expression of the fact that Torah is the source of life.[3] The Ḥayyim Palachi held a noble ethical conception regarding the dissemination of Torah; he customarily distributed his books gratis to Torah scholars and did not sell them for personal profit.[1, 3] Each time he completed writing a book, he customarily held a festive se'udat mitzvah.[1]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Phenomenology of Segulot, Dreams, and His Final Days

Rabbi Ḥayyim Palachi received tremendous veneration among the masses, who regarded him as a holy man and turned to him for blessings and segulot.[13, 14] The Ḥayyim Palachi incorporated in his compositions a variety of segulot and prayers intended to ease the suffering of those who approached him.[3, 13, 14]

Among the famous segulot he documented is his well-known segulah for nullifying alien and evil thoughts during prayer, by reciting three verses seven times in succession: "A perpetual fire shall burn upon the altar, it shall not go out"; "I hate divided thoughts, but Your Torah I love"; and "How fair and pleasant you are, O loved one, delectable maiden."[13]

Another famous segulah, designated for the eve of the festival of Shavu'ot, instructs one to set aside a sum of 91 perutot (corresponding to the numerical value of "amen" and "mal'akh") and to complete it to the measure of twice the word "ben" in gemaṭria, equaling 104 perutot, and to give them to a poor and humble Torah scholar.[15] The Ḥayyim Palachi emphasized that this act constitutes a rectification for the sin of Adam, the sin of the Golden Calf, and the blemish of the covenant, and even serves as a segulah for the childless and brings the redemption closer.[15] Likewise, the Ḥayyim Palachi attributed great importance to the power of the prayer "Aleinu le-shabbe'aḥ" recited with proper intention, and promised that a person who does so is proven and tested to be saved from his troubles.[14]

The Ḥayyim Palachi's mystical conception was also expressed in his attitude toward dreams; he merited numerous revelations from Heaven through dreams, and noted in introductions to his books (such as Pe'ulat Ṣaddiq le-Ḥayyim, Lev Ḥayyim, and Kaf ha-Ḥayyim) that the titles of his books and various halakhic allusions were transmitted to him in night dreams as heavenly confirmation of his Torah endeavor, and he was even warned in his dreams of harsh decrees destined to come upon the community.[3, 6]

In his final days the Ḥayyim Palachi continued leading the community and writing continuously, despite the heavy public burden he bore upon his shoulders.[6] On the night before his passing, the Ḥayyim Palachi performed tikkun ḥaṣot and wept bitterly over the exile of the Shekhinah and the suffering of Israel.[6] On the 15th of Shevat 5628 he completed his final spiritual rectification upon earth, and on the 17th of Shevat 5628 (February 10, 1868), at eighty years of age, he returned his soul to his Creator.[1, 2, 6]

The Ḥayyim Palachi's funeral was an unprecedented display of honor in the history of Turkish Jewry. The funeral procession was attended by masses of people from the Jewish community, the rabbis of Izmir, and public figures.[1, 3, 6] Out of special and profound respect for his accomplishments, the Ottoman government sent official representatives and military personnel who accompanied his coffin, alongside diplomatic representatives from foreign countries.[1, 3, 6] The Ḥayyim Palachi was interred in the ancient Jewish cemetery "Bahari Baba" in Izmir, and subsequently his grave was transferred to the sages' section in the "Gürçeşme" cemetery in the city, a site that serves to this day as a center for pilgrimage and prayer for masses of the House of Israel who seek to be remembered through the merit of the Torah giant of Izmir.[2, 16]
